name: CIOMS Working Group XIV on AI in Pharmacovigilance
blurb: International guidance on AI in drug safety.
title: CIOMS Working Group XIV on AI in Pharmacovigilance
answer: CIOMS Working Group XIV brought regulators and industry together to set principles for AI in pharmacovigilance. Its report treats AI tools that influence patient safety as needing governance close to that applied to medicines themselves: risk based validation, human oversight, transparency and continuous monitoring.

reading.body:
CIOMS Working Group XIV produced consensus guidance, not regulation, that treats AI tools affecting patient safety as needing governance close to that applied to medicines.

The pattern is that governance arrives before enforcement. The report sets out risk based validation, human oversight, transparency and continuous monitoring, and it carries weight because regulators took part in writing it rather than because any authority can compel it. A safety team can adopt it as the backbone of an internal AI policy and use it as a shared vocabulary in inspection discussions.

For AI specifically, the significance is where the guidance places these tools. A model that influences patient safety is treated less like software and more like a medicine, which means validation and monitoring obligations attach to the tool itself and persist after deployment. That is a different posture from treating AI as a productivity layer over existing pharmacovigilance work.

The data does not say which regulators participated, which jurisdictions have adopted the principles, or how they interact with binding rules such as the EU AI Act. It records one development, the report's publication, and no compliance deadline or enforcement action. Nothing here speaks to compute, buildings or power, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

The report's scope is broader than validation of a single model. It names five distinct obligations, and they map onto different stages of a tool's life: appropriateness decisions before build, validation before deployment, oversight during operation, transparency toward regulators, and privacy and fairness across the data the tool touches. A safety team that reads the guidance as a checklist for model selection will miss the parts that apply after go-live.

The comparison the data supports is between two ways of classifying the same software. Treated as a productivity layer, an AI tool is a feature of the pharmacovigilance workflow and its failures are workflow failures. Treated as close to a medicine, the tool carries its own validation and monitoring obligations that survive deployment, and its failures are safety events. The guidance takes the second position for any tool that influences patient safety, which is a category defined by effect rather than by technical sophistication.

The practical consequence is that the governance burden scales with what the tool can change, not with how advanced it is. A simple model that touches a safety decision falls inside the principles, and a sophisticated one that never does may not. That inverts the usual procurement instinct of scrutinizing the most complex systems hardest.

Is the CIOMS report a regulation?
No. It is consensus guidance, but it carries weight because regulators contributed to it.

How do I get the report?
It is available from CIOMS, linked in the developments above.

Which regulators took part in Working Group XIV?
The data does not name them. It says only that regulators, industry and academics were brought together and that regulators helped write the report.

Which jurisdictions have adopted these principles?
The data does not say. It records the report's publication and no adoption by any authority.

How does the guidance interact with the EU AI Act?
The data does not address the interaction. The EU AI Act appears only as a related term on the page, not as a rule the report is described as connecting to.

Does the report set a compliance deadline?
No deadline appears in the data. The only dated event is the report's publication, and no enforcement action is recorded.

What does the guidance require of a tool that influences patient safety?
Risk based validation, human oversight, transparency and continuous monitoring, with data privacy and fairness also covered. The report also addresses how to decide where AI is appropriate in the first place.

explainer:
The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences is an international body that brings regulators, industry and academics together to write consensus guidance on drug safety and research. Its working group reports, for example on safety reporting and benefit risk, have shaped regulatory practice worldwide for decades.

Working Group XIV addressed artificial intelligence in pharmacovigilance. Its report covers how to decide where AI is appropriate, how to validate and monitor AI tools, what human oversight is needed, how to manage transparency and explainability, and how to handle data privacy and fairness. Because regulators helped write it, it gives companies a widely recognised basis for their own policies and a common language for inspection discussions.

What CIOMS is and why its working groups matter

The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences is a non governmental body founded under the World Health Organization and UNESCO. Its working groups bring regulators, industry and academics together to write consensus reports, and in pharmacovigilance those reports have shaped practice for decades: the CIOMS report form for adverse events, periodic safety reporting, signal detection and benefit risk assessment all trace to earlier working groups. A CIOMS report is not law, but regulators cite it and inspectors expect companies to know it.

What Working Group XIV addresses

The group's remit is AI in pharmacovigilance: where it can be used, what principles should govern it, and how to validate and oversee it. The themes it works through include human oversight, transparency about what a model does, validity and robustness of models over time, fairness across patient groups, data privacy, and governance and accountability inside the company. It aims to give companies and regulators a shared framework rather than a technical standard.

How companies are using it

Even before the final report, safety teams have been aligning their AI governance to the group's principles so that their validation documents and inspection answers use the same language regulators will recognise. The practical effect is to turn a question an inspector might ask in many ways into one the company has already answered in a recognised framework. When the report is final, it will likely become the reference that safety AI programmes are measured against.
